long_biography.plain_text:
After an online-gaming venture failed, Nick Woodman went surfing in Australia and Indonesia. He returned with a practical problem to solve: how could an amateur photograph himself in the water? He developed a wrist strap around a compact film camera, sold imported shell belts for working capital and received substantial loans from his parents. The combination made GoPro a founder-built company with a materially advantaged launch.

Woodman founded GoPro in 2002 and developed the HERO from a film camera into a digital action-camera system supported by mounts and user-created video. He took the company public in 2014 and remains its chairman and chief executive. A dual-class structure gives him majority voting power through shares held personally and by a family trust, but voting control is not the same as owning GoPro's assets. He later sold large blocks of stock. Compounded returns on those proceeds now account for most of his personal fortune, although no separately documented family-office firm was verified.
